The most recent economic signals are mixed, however and although one swallow does not a summer make, the April employment figures from the United States were strong enough to give commodities some support as the markets regained a degree of risk appetite. While the non-farm payroll figures were themselves stronger, with a gain of 244,000 in April against expectations of +185,000, they were interpreted as doubly supportive for gold. The first element is the revival of risk appetite for commodities. The second, though, is that _unemployment_ rose to 9%, since unemployment is the key, at present, to the determination of Federal Reserve Chairman Bernanke to keep US interest rates as low as possible for as long as feasible inorder to try and stimulate the economy. This is a driving theme through our expectations for higher gold prices towards year-end as the global economy starts to reap the results of ultra-loose monetary policy (and probably also helps to inform the continued increase of central banks in the gold market; see page Au3). Meanwhile we are looking for a small rebound in the dollar:euro rate in coming weeks, but do not believe that this will be the start of a secular recovery in the tradeweighted dollar. The dollar was under persistent pressure in the latter part of April, responding bearishly both to good economic news and associated appetite for risk, and also to poorer news, notably with respect to sovereign debt. The dollar suffered from bouts of economic confidence during April in that increased risk appetite encouraged the dollar carry trade in favour of higher-yielding assets. Europe is suffering in particular over continued fears about sovereign debt while S&P investors are caught between good corporate results and fears of sovereign debt contagion_ Following the April meeting, at the inaugural quarterly Press Conference from the Federal Reserve, Chairman Bernanke said that the stimulus programme [the $600bn of bondbuying, plus up to $200bn of reinvestment in mortgage repayments and other maturing assets] would be completed this June and implied that he remains averse to raising interest rates for as long as possible, subject to inflationary pres

sures. Until the minutes are released (19th May), we are unlikely to gauge the degree of consensus and this most recent meeting (subject of course to individual speeches from any of the Federal board governors or bank presidents) implies continued uncertainty among Fed watchers. The Fed’s inflation forecasts currently centre on a range between 1% and 2% from now to 2013. This has caused some raised eyebrows among Fed watchers with a number of commentators opining that the Fed is perhaps too sanguine in its belief that inflationary pressures are transient. GFMS counts itself among those who are sceptical about this view from the Fed and this one reason why we believe gold has another bull leg in it. Gold thrives not only on inflationary forces, but also on discord at the top; it does rather look as if it will enjoy the benefits of both in coming months. The intraday high trades were reportedly between $1,576 and $1,578 on 2nd May, while the lows were between $1,480 and $1,485 on 5th May, a fall of roughly $90 or 6%. The speed of the move, and the publicity that has been associated with it, perhaps masks the fact that in early May, at just under $1,500/oz gold was only at three-week lows. The price rise in April had been steep, extending the most recent bull leg that had started in early February, and then paused for a period of consolidation during much of March. This renewed rise in price was underlain by a shifting pattern of demand, which is detailed below, but which involved some investors changing their stance and taking the view that, although the price was already at historic highs, it was destined for further gains; some were therefore re-entering the market. Elsewhere demand had subsided and there was also evidence of scrap flows from some areas so the demand-side infra-structure, at the private investment level at least, was showing some signs of fracture. Other news that has given the market a talking point is the fresh acquisition of gold by the Bank of Mexico. This is likely to prompt the debate between a) those who might argue that these purchases formed physical support for gold in the first quarter of the year and who may question whether this support has now waned; and b) those who would argue that this highlights gold’s attraction to those central banks that have small gold allocations and who are looking to increase their tonnage as their foreign exchange reserves continue to swell. At GFMS we have inclined towards the latter argument for some time and we are still expecting the official sector to be a reasonably substantial net purchaser this year. This is discussed further below. **Outlook; pause for breath, risk of further weakness in mid-year, but an attack on $1,600 before year-end** Gold started April with a fix of $1,434.50 and rallied to $1,470 in the first week before correcting and then pushing on to cle

ar $1,500 in the third week (following the Standard & Poor’s downgrade of the United States’ credit outlook and higher Chinese inflation than the market had expected). The high fix to date of $1546.50 marked a gain of 11% since the start of this year and of 33% over a twelve month period.
